section.title: Introduction
section.para: The package opennlp.tools.pii finds personally identifiable mentions as exact spans over the original text. A PiiAnnotator writes the opennlp:pii layer from a PiiExtractor; the built-in CursorPiiExtractor recognizes email addresses, phone numbers, IBANs, and payment card numbers, each with a type constant and a normalized form. Numeric types are checksum validated, and an IBAN candidate must additionally match the ISO 13616 registry: a registered country code and exactly the length that country assigns, so a checksum-passing run with an unknown country or a wrong length is not reported. Email domains must end in an IANA-registered top-level domain (including punycode forms) and stay within the RFC 1035 presentation-length limit, so private-use suffixes such as .internal or .local are not reported. The ASCII local part is capped at 64 characters and the complete mailbox at 254 characters. Local-part case is preserved in the normalized form, while the case-insensitive domain is lowercased. The baked IANA snapshot is refreshed with dev/fetch-iana-tlds.sh; pass --check in an automated drift check without changing the source tree. The calling-code and IBAN length tables are regenerated from libphonenumber and the SWIFT registry with dev/fetch-phone-number-lengths.sh and dev/fetch-iban-lengths.sh, respectively. An extractor limited to a subset of the types, for a caller that wants only payment data found, is built with new CursorPiiExtractor(Set.of(PiiMention.TYPE_CARD)).

Further detectors, for network addresses, credentials, cryptocurrency addresses, bank routing numbers, national identifiers, and device identifiers, are opt-in and described under Opt-in detectors and packs. None of them is part of CursorPiiExtractor, so what a caller already redacts never changes when a detector is added.

section.title: Annotating and masking
section.para:
A MaskPolicy controls how the covered characters are replaced while staying length preserving. keepingFormat() leaves separators visible so the kind of value stays recognizable, and keepingTrailing(4) leaves the last four letters or digits of each span readable, the customary receipt style. PiiUsageExampleTest asserts the exact output shown here.
String receipt = Masker.mask(document, PiiAnnotator.PII, MaskPolicy.of('*').keepingFormat().keepingTrailing(4)); // "Contact ****@******e.com, call (***) ***-4567, or charge card **** **** **** 1111."

What is customary differs by type, and MaskPolicies collects those defaults: a card keeps its last four digits, an address or an IP address keeps only its separators, and a credential is masked whole, formatting included, since even its shape says which system it opens. Passing the defaults to Masker chooses a policy per mention, so one pass redacts a mixed document correctly.
String masked = Masker.mask(document, PiiAnnotator.PII, MaskPolicies.byType()); // "Contact ****@*******.***, call (***) ***-****, or charge card **** **** **** 1111."

section.title: Opt-in detectors and packs
section.para: CursorPiiExtractor reports email addresses, phone numbers, IBANs, and payment card numbers, and it always will: adding a type to it would silently change what every existing caller redacts. Everything else is opt-in, in extractors that each validate against the standard they implement rather than against a shape.

listitem.para: NetworkPiiExtractor: IPv4, IPv6, and MAC addresses.

SecretsPiiExtractor: AWS access key identifiers, GitHub tokens from their current minimum lengths through the 255-character scanner limit, JSON Web Tokens whose header decodes to a JWS header, and credentials embedded in a URL.
CryptoPiiExtractor: Bitcoin addresses, legacy Base58Check and segwit bech32 or bech32m, and Ethereum addresses with the EIP-55 checksum where the case carries one.

UsIdentityPiiExtractor, EuIdentityPiiExtractor, and CaIdentityPiiExtractor: United States Social Security and taxpayer numbers, United Kingdom NHS numbers, the German tax identifier, and context-labeled Canadian Social Insurance Numbers. National identifiers are the most context dependent of the lot, which is why they are never on by default.
DevicePiiExtractor: 15-digit, Luhn-valid IMEIs that directly follow an IMEI label. The label prevents a generic long number from becoming a device identifier by checksum alone.

section.title: Pseudonymizing, tokenizing, and auditing
section.para:
Labels number from one in every text, so they say nothing across documents. Where that is the question, HmacTokenizer derives the label from the value under a secret key, and the same address tokenizes identically in every document. A plain digest of a value drawn from a small space, a Social Security number for instance, is recovered by digesting the space. The secret key prevents that attack, and it must contain at least 32 random bytes. Tokens made under one key are deliberately linkable, so they remain pseudonymous data and logs containing them still require access control.
HmacTokenizer tokenizer = new HmacTokenizer(key); // at least 32 random bytes
String stable = tokenizer.token(PiiMention.TYPE_EMAIL, "jane@example.com"); // "EMAIL-3f2a1c9d7e4b6a20", the same in every document scanned under this key
String tokenized = tokenizer.rewrite(document).text();
